one or another difficulty of computation (a complaint I have with much
of the literature in Stochastic Thermodynamics). The structure of the
Methods and the SI is also conscientious and makes the paper
sufficiently self-contained that it can be read without too much
detailed back-referencing to specific constructions in the citations.
I did not find any errors in the constructions or claimed results,
apart from some small typographic lapses, though there is a lot in
this paper, and it will take me more weeks than I have to complete
this review to be sure I can reproduce every equation here. So in
that sense I have not done the complete check I would normally want to
do.
We appreciate the kind words.
-- I won't ask for any change on the following point, but as a comment
from a reader to the Authors, I am unconvinced that the Lagrange
multiplier on dwelling fractions pi is a counterpart in NEQ to the
"First Law" (energy conservation) for EQ. It looks more like what it
exactly is (on the state space): the conservation of a probability
measure and its dual Lagrange multiplier, which is uniform on all
states. As Schnakenberg observes in his constructions, probability
migration on the state space is equivalent to number conservation for
particles in a linear master equation, so probability conservation in
NEQ plays the same role as number (N) conservation in EQ.
For all the models in this paper, which describe random walkers on
simple graphs, one can lift from the lattice of many-particle states
to the graph of one-particle states (many-particle partition functions
simply factor), so an ambiguity is allowed in which level of "state"
one is referring to. In a system with stoichiometry, however (among
many other cases), probability on the state space would not convert to
anything simple and general on the graphs of chemical species, and we
would see that probability conservation is not performing the same
kind of constraint on state occupancies that number conservation
performs, or that energy conservation performs in open systems.
That distinction gets sharper if we consider partition functions to be
the truly fundamental entities, and the treatment of probabilities to
be an ex-post and arbitrary normalization convention. In EQ, (U,V,N)
still impose (structured) constraints on state occupancies in the
partition function, but if they are absent for NEQ, I don't see
anything else that takes their place.
So I don't dispute that the construction here goes through as
demonstrated, and I am glad to have it. But I am not sure the
conceptual correspondence is the one the Authors assert (here and in
earlier work). It is an important question in general, because the
extensive arguments to the entropy in EQ get their privileged status
through one or another conservation law (due to symmetry or
otherwise), and it seems to me still a very open question whether
there is anything different from conservation laws, which plays the
same role in relation to extended-time distributions, that
conservation plays for state ensemble.
This is a deep, insightful and important point. Although no change was requested on this point,
their comment prompted us to further strengthen our manuscript’s central arguments for a broad
readership. We have made two key revisions:
First, we expanded the main text to more explicitly justify the distinctness of the observables (π,
τ, J) and the completeness of the basis it forms. This added detail adds clarities to the First Law of
Completeness we propose and reinforces why all three components are essential.
Second, we agree that extending this to interacting systems is a critical future step, which we now
note in our newly added outlook in the last paragraph before the Summary. In short, we believe
developing approaches in coarse graining or perturbative, cluster expansion-like expansion of
interaction might be useful next steps.
-- I will comment that I found the paper somewhat frustrating and hard
to read in the first few passes, though perhaps this is unavoidable
due to the Nature emphasis on brevity ahead of all other
considerations. Because anything said anywhere is never repeated
again, unless one has a mathematician's eidetic memory for notation,
one has to have three windows open at the same time, to read the text,
its associated methods sections, and the SI section. I eventually
decided that the authors do consistently use the terms "transition
rates", "posterior transition rates", and just "rates" to refer to the
quantities k_{ij}, and "probability edge flux" to refer to the 1-way
currents pi_i k_{ij} through edges. But as a shorthand when computing
examples, these rates get several different sets of names, and in
Fig.4 and Fig.M2 the annotations make them look like the fluxes pi_i
k_{ij} rather than just the k_{ij} factors in those fluxes. And of
course r_i is overloaded with the components in the right eigenvector
of the tilted transition matrix, which appears in the general
posterior evaluation of k_{ij}.
Maybe there is nothing I should ask the authors to do. But would it
make it easier for readers to interpret the English terms
mathematically without wondering whether they are assuming the correct
quantities, if the Authors could just add a few words to note that "in
this example the rates k_{ij} will be denoted f_i, r_i for brevity",
and possibly find a typographical convention where these r_i terms
aren't denoted the same way as right eigenvector coefficients.
We have now expanded the main text to make it more accessible and self-consistent. We have
now added texts when Fig. 3 and 4 are first mentioned (line 286-288 and line 326-328) and also in
the caption of Fig. M2 to explain the f, r, and f’ variables are shorthand notations for k_ij. We now
use u_i and v_i for left and right eigenvectors.
-- There are a few small typographic problems that need a better
proofread. I probably won't capture every one I saw here, but, e.g.:
l.705--706 double +
SI l.235 old notation beta_1 + beta_2 not updated to beta_c + beta_m
Mostly the equations are strikingly clean and free of errors, and also
very elegantly reduced to terms with intuitive meanings.
Thanks. We have corrected the double + (now at line 799) and the betas (now at line 173 of the
revised SI).
I would recommend that the second Author do a proofread of the SI,
just for sentence structure and English composition at several points
(probably ~10 across the whole SI). These things don't harm
comprehensibility, but they suggest a senior author who kind of
checked out of the process when he was convinced the main results were
okay, as if the paper didn't deserve the last little bit of
follow-through.
From the senior author: Guilty as charged. I have now edited.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors introduce two new laws for nonequilibrium stat mech,
building upon the Caliber force theory. Specifically, the first law states that a steady-
state nonequilibrium system can be fully characterized by distributions and fluxes. The
second law establishes the Maximum Caliber principle, which defines caliber forces,
i.e., conjugate forces derived from path entropy. Here, Caliber is analogous to the
logarithm of the partition function in equilibrium stat mech. Overall, the authors put
forward an ambitious framework that could serve as the foundation for a new set of
nonequilibrium theories, such as Maxwell-like relations and fluctuation–response
relations for fluxes and conjugate forces, etc. To demonstrate the capability of their two-
law framework, they apply it to several simple systems, such as ATP/ADP energy
transport and stochastic transport in a circuit.
While these theories may well be correct and their applications indeed highlight their
promise, we still couldn’t fully grasp the definition of Caliber force from a fundamental
perspective. In classical thermodynamics, a force is defined as the partial derivative of
the logarithm of the partition functon(or free energy), e.g., F=-kT\partial ln Z/\partial x. In
contrast, Caliber forces are defined as the partial derivatives of the path entropy (Eq.
(3)) rather than the free energy. In their framework, the free energy is the Caliber (see
Eq. (5)). However, if we were to define forces as derivatives of the Caliber, the result
seems inconsistent, leading to the form (F=F+\partial s_path) according to Eq. (4). This
inconsistency is puzzling to us.
We think the main problem here was just that our earlier text did not communicate clearly. We
have now revised the manuscript to clarify this “entropy-first” approach, which follows the
foundational perspective of pioneers like Callen, Landau, and Jaynes. Our reasoning is twofold:
First, and most fundamentally, this definition is essential for establishing the predictive
tendency relationships that are the hallmark of a thermodynamic theory. The monotonic response
of an observable (like volume, V) to a change in its conjugate variable (like P/T) arises directly
from the concavity of the entropy function. Defining our forces as entropy derivatives is what
guarantees these powerful, predictive relationships hold far from equilibrium in our framework.
More specifically, the concavity of entropy means the entropy derivatives (1/T, P/T, - mu/T) and
coordinate (U,V,N) have monotonic relationships–––increasing one variable (e.g. mu/T or P/T)
while fixing the other is guaranteed to always increase or decrease (depend on sign convention)
its conjugate (e.g. N or V).
This can also be understood from a dual perspective. This monotonicity is connected to the
fluctuation-susceptibility equalities. The Caliber (or the log-partition function in EQ) is the
generating function for the system’s statistical cumulants. Its second derivative with respect to a
force variable gives the variance of the conjugate observable—a quantity that must be positive.
For example, in canonical ensemble, the average energy <E> = - d (ln Z) / d(beta) where beta =
1/T. The fluctuation is Var(E)= d^2 (lnZ)/d (beta)^2. This leads to d <E> / d (beta) = - Var(E),
thus the monotonicity. The relation d <E> / dT = Var(E) / (k_B T^2) comes after, by substituting
beta = 1/T. The monotonicity of thermodynamic conjugacy comes from the log-partition function
being a function of the “force variables.”
Second, the alternative and more familiar definition of force as a spatial gradient of free energy
has two significant limitations in the context of a general non-equilibrium theory. (1) It relies on a
local-equilibrium approximation, which is fundamentally an approximation that breaks down
far from equilibrium. The concept is EQ-based, with unclear path for far-from-EQ generalizations.
(2) It provides an incomplete description of flow control. As we now illustrate with the “battery
and circuit” analogy in the revised text (first paragraph of Discussion), it only captures the overall
driving force (the “battery”) and neglects the crucial conductive properties of the pathway (the
“circuit”), which our complete set of node and edge forces is designed to describe.
For these reasons, our “entropy-first” definition is a deliberate choice to build a framework that is
more general, complete, and has the robust mathematical structure required for a predictive non-
equilibrium theory. We have added a detailed discussion of this principled choice to the Discussion
section of our manuscript.
The framework of Caliber force relies on the assumption of Markov dynamics, i.e., that
transitions along each segment of a path are Markovian. However, this assumption may
not hold for realistic biological systems, including the ATP hydrolysis driven molecular
motors, when detailed molecular mechanisms are taken into account. In the SI, the
authors discuss possible extensions of their theory to non-Markovian dynamics. The
first approach involves discrete-time Markov State Models (MSMs), which require
sufficiently long lag times to render the dynamics Markovian. This seems reasonable,
given the large community already applying MSMs to protein dynamics. The second
approach relies on higher-order Markov chains, where finite memory effects are
explicitly considered. It remains unclear to me, however, how their framework can be
consistently extended to such higher-order chains. In any case, this important issue
needs to be discussed in the main text, rather than being confined to the SI.
We thank the reviewer for their feedback. We have now moved the discussion previously in the
SI to the Method section (now Method K). We have also expanded the non-Markov discussion by
including more explanatory text (line 959-980). In short, converting a higher-order Markov to a
first-order one is like converting the second-order Newton’s equation of position x to a first-order
system of equations of position and velocity. For discrete time, we consider the augmented state,
e.g. 𝑍 = (𝑌,𝑌 ) to map a second-order problem back to first-order. We have also added an
t_t_t-1
outlook paragraph near the end of the Discussion section (line 415-423) to showcase to the readers
this and other exciting future opportunities CFT points to.
Several minor comments:
When deriving the Maxwell-like equation (Eq. 8(a) and (b)), the authors did not explain
what x_1 and x_2 (or F_1 and F_2) represent. The notion of a “mixed coordinate”
involving x_1 and F_2 is also not clarified. Are they two sub degrees of the system?
Could the authors provide some explanations?
We have now added explanatory text before Eq. 8. Mixed coordinates is like switching to the
canonical ensemble (T,V,N) from microcanonical ensemble (U,V,N)–––we switch out conjugated
variables U and 1/T. Similarly, an example for (F1, x2) would be F1=Fcycle and x2 = (pi, tau).
Could the authors clarify each term of the tilted matrix in the equation at Line 584 (not
numbered), and explain how each term is derived from Fig. M1a? In particular, there are
two edges between nodes 2 and 3 in Fig. M1a; do these correspond to F and F’ in the
tilted matrix? Furthermore, Fig. M1a appears symmetric for edges 1->2 and 1->3, so
why is M_12 significantly different from M_13?
We have now expanded the introductory texts near the previous line 584 (now around line 663).
Yes. This is what we meant by “F23 is the edge force on the diagonal 23 and F’23 is that on the
curved 23.”
M_12 and M_13 are different because the first fundamental cycle flux uses 12 as the defining
edge (chord)–––that is, the fundamental cycle flux J_c1 = p_12 – p_21. The edge 13, on the
other hand, is not measured because that would have been redundant–––the net flux from 3 to 1
must equal to the net flux from 1 to 2 at nonequilibrium steady state.
Reviewer 6
This is a theoretical manuscript on the maximum caliber principle, focusing on the
calibers of steady-state systems, along with the concepts of caliber force and Maxwell-
Onsager relations. The authors first propose two laws for non-equilibrium dynamics: the
first law says three types of variables are sufficient to describe a path, and the second
law establishes the principle of maximum caliber. Based on these laws, the manuscript
introduces the concept of caliber forces, defined as the partial derivative of the path
entropy with respect to these variables. Unlike conventional path-based theories that
consider variations of paths in space, this manuscript treats the path as fixed and uses
the maximum caliber principle to compute physical quantities along it. Then this
manuscript employs large deviation theory to evaluate the calibers, deriving a second-
order relation that leads to a Maxwell-Onsager-like relation. Finally, two applications of
the caliber force framework are presented: ATP/ADP energy transport and an analogue
of Kirchhoff's third law for circuits.
This manuscript presents an interesting and novel application of the
maximum caliber principle to physical systems. A straightforward use of
this principle typically focuses on identifying the optimal path within a
path ensemble, where the physical properties of each path can be analytically obtained.
In contrast, this work offers a different perspective to vary the physical properties along
fixed paths, rather than varying the paths. This insightful approach has the potential to
significantly broaden the scope of applications of the maximum caliber principle.
However, I have serious concerns about the theoretical foundation of this
manuscript, and I am not yet convinced that the proposed framework is fully consistent with
fundamental principles of physics.
Here again, we believe our previous text was not sufficiently clear, and have now fixed it. We
make three key points:
• Role of Max Cal: We use Max Cal here not to find an “optimal path,” but as a variational
principle for building a path probability model that has the desired conjugate variable
structure. In this process, paths are integrated over, not individually varied. We vary the
candidate path probability instead. One can of course identify a path, e.g. the most probable
one, based on the built path probability model.
• Novelty: The novelty of our work is in combining this Max Cal principle with a First Law
of completeness, obtaining forces and conjugate relations and Legendre Transforming
variables and constraints. This elevates Max Cal from a method of building a model (as
statmech would do in EQ) into a complete, constructive theory that gives conjugate
relationships for all possible processes on a given state space network (as the laws of
thermodynamics do for EQ).
• Consistency and new integration: Our framework is fully self-consistent, built directly
on the mathematics of LDT and Max Cal, and it roots the cycle affinity from Stochastic
Thermodynamics (ST) in a principled cycle force. We note that this integration among
LDT, Max Cal, and ST is new.
Traditionally, the caliber is defined as the quantity called as path entropy in this
manuscript. Rather than maximizing the path entropy, the authors introduce a new
definition of caliber as the Legendre transform of the path entropy, and then propose a
maximum principle for this new quantity. For non-equilibrium systems such as the
steady states studied in this paper, it may indeed be reasonable that this new form of
caliber, rather than the path entropy, is the quantity being maximized. However, this
crucial explanation is missing, which makes the proposed principle difficult to
understand.
We now clarify. Think of EQ statmech. You can either maximize the entropy subject to
constraints, or you can just minimize the free energy (because the constraints are already included.)
They are exactly equivalent. It’s true here too, and we now spell that out. See texts after Eq. 4
and line 645-648 in Method E.
The authors neither provide a proof nor demonstrate consistency with existing theories
for the maximum principle of the caliber as defined in this manuscript. Instead, they rely
on an analogy with statistical mechanics to support their framework. However, this
analogy is difficult to understand.
First, what existing theories? We do describe how CFT uses past Max Cal and LDT and how it
goes beyond limitations in Stochastic Thermodynamics. We’ve now added more context of other
work in the Discussion section. But second, our reference to EQ statmech is in no way a
justification of anything. It is just a metaphor to communicate to an audience that is already
familiar with Thermo and for whom the present work can be quite unfamiliar.
Since the caliber force is a key component in the definition of caliber in this manuscript,
let's first examine the formulation of the caliber force. The authors define caliber forces
as derivatives of path entropies. However, in statistical mechanics, derivatives of
entropy are not forces. For example, in the Maxwell relation, \partial S/\partial V=\partial
P/\partial T, while P can be regarded as the conjugate force of V, \partial S/\partial V is
not P but rather a partial derivative of P.
The manuscript then introduces a Legendre transform of the path entropy to define the
caliber, which is presented as analogous to the logarithm of the partition function or the
free energy in thermodynamics. If this analogy holds, shouldn't the conjugate force be
defined instead as the partial derivative of the caliber c, i.e. F=\partial c/\partial x,
just like in thermodynamics where F=\partial A/\partial x, where the free energy A=-kT ln Z?
Defining forces as derivatives of entropy is essential for the forces to have the right tendency
relations to the observables. This point is similar to a concern from Reviewer 4, which we have
provided a more comprehensive explanation (please also see our first response to reviewer 4). In
brief, the tendency predictions in EQ comes from the conjugate relations between “forces” (1/T,
P/T) and the observables (U,V), which originates from the concavity of the entropy function. The
“free energy gradient” picture has two limitations for NEQ flows: (1) it rests on a local-equilibrium
approximation, and (2) it only provides an incomplete “end-control” to flows.
Furthermore, as the caliber is analogue to free energy in equilibrium dynamics, why
should the caliber involving cycle flux that corresponds to a non-equilibrium system still
satisfy the maximum caliber principle, as the minimal free energy rule only applies to
equilibrium thermodynamics?
Our new Method C now explains this.
Max Cal as a method of model inference holds for generic stochastic dynamics, detailed balance
or not. Given a set of observable constraints, it generates a family of processes that has the desired
conjugate variables and relationships. This is parallel to the conjugate structure in EQ, which
comes from the Boltzmann probability distribution maximizing state entropy under average
constraints. Gibbs’ statistical physics showed that conjugate structure comes from the maximum
entropy (or Caliber) principle. Jaynes was the one who point out it comes from the principle being
used as a variational principle, for building models with conjugate structure.
The part missing in past Max Cal is that that family of models it generates from an arbitrary set of
observables does not cover all possible processes. I.e., we didn’t have the right observable set to
describe all processes of interest. That is where the First Law of completeness comes in: it enables
that family of dynamics to cover all possible dynamics. Thus, by combining the two laws, we have
made any stochastic dynamics (detailed balance or not) a member of the exponential family and
possess the desired conjugate relations.
Therefore, detailed explanations and validations of their theoretical framework are
needed, especially for the definition of the caliber forces, the definition of the caliber c
(as the Legendre transformation of path entropy), and the maximum principle of caliber
c. The analogy should be fully consistent with the existing theories in physics. For the
validations, I suggest that authors can provide rigorous proof or consistency with
existing theories when studying the same problems.
We thank the reviewer for these suggestions. We have now added texts to provide clearer
reasonings in the main text, a new Method C for the technical justification, remarks on the
definition of the Caliber, and how our framework relates to past Max Cal (and other framework)
in the Discussion section of the main text.
In addition, I have some minor concerns of this manuscript.
This manuscript focuses only on simple illustrative examples, such as the two-node two-edge model of ATP/ADP energy transport. In reality, the ATP/ADP system involves proteins with a large number of degrees of freedom. A Markov model of such molecular systems would necessarily contain a large number of nodes and edges. While in this manuscript each term and the eigenvalues of the tilted matrix are derived analytically, could the authors discuss how their framework could be extended to handle the Markov models with large numbers of nodes and edges for realistic systems?
Scaling up is indeed an exciting next step after we formulate the foundations here. We have
discussed several directions in a new outlook paragraph near the end of the Discussion section
(right before Summary). In short, we note that the traffic variables are perfect for identifying fast
interconverting states for temporal coarse graining and actually have been used by others to get
metastable groups of states. For tackling interactions, we remark potential synergies with other
frameworks.
The authors argue that the EPR rule fails. In the main text, they state that EPR provides
conjugate forces of fluxes only in the linear-response regime. While this limitation is
valid, it is not a failure. Since path entropy is rooted in equilibrium systems, it is natural
that its non- equilibrium extension would only reproduce near-equilibrium results. The
caliber force theory may indeed aim to extend beyond the near-equilibrium regime, but
as argued above, such an extension requires rigorous validations.
Thanks. We have revised our statement. The text now clarifies that “the EPR is not a general
variational potential” outside the linear-response regime. This accurately reflects its limitations
without dismissing its validity in the appropriate context, and better highlights the need for the
more general potential provided by our framework.

### Reviewer 1

The authors have addressed some of my earlier concerns, and I appreciate their efforts in revising the manuscript. However,
my main concern regarding the novelty and conceptual contribution of the work remains unresolved. Below, I summarize
several points that, in my view, still require clarification or further development.
On the claimed variational principle
The authors examine a Markovian dynamical process (as suggested by the transition from Eq. 2a to Eq. 2b) by fixing
stationary probabilities, traffic, and cycle fluxes, and they show that the path entropy of this process has a mathematical form
reminiscent of thermodynamic potentials in equilibrium statistical mechanics. However, there seems to be a conceptual
misunderstanding here.
In equilibrium thermodynamics, specifying macroscopic quantities such as U,V,N is sufficient to predict macroscopic
behavior because these quantities are complete descriptors at that level; the underlying microscopic distributions are
determined by maximizing the entropy subject to these constraints. In contrast, the authors’ framework specifies
probabilities, traffics, and fluxes, which together fully determine the microscopic dynamics (Eq. 1). If the microscopic
dynamics are already fixed, then there is no remaining degree of freedom over which to maximize the path entropy, and thus
no variational principle in the usual MaxEnt or MaxCal sense. In that light, describing this formalism as a “dynamical
equivalent” of maximizing state entropy is misleading, since Caliber (or entropy) is typically maximized to infer unknown
distributions rather than to restate known ones.
On the state, traffic, flux decomposition
The proposed decomposition appears somewhat arbitrary. As the authors note, it is equivalent to specifying all transition
rates, which fully determine the dynamics. One could, in principle, derive the equivalent of Eq. 3 directly in terms of the
transition rates k_ij. Moreover, a force-flux formalism could be defined with respect to any rank-preserving linear
transformation of the rate constants. Therefore, it is not clear why this particular decomposition should be regarded as
fundamental.
On the interpretation of the “force-flux” relationship
The claim that Eq. 3 represents a relationship between cycle affinity and cycle flux may be misleading. In classical
nonequilibrium thermodynamics, force-flux relationships connect measurable thermodynamic forces (differences in
temperature, chemical potential, etc.) to observable fluxes (e.g. of heat or matter). In contrast, in the current formalism the
“forces” are defined in terms of microscopic quantities and are not externally tunable. As a result, the physical meaning or
utility of these forces is difficult to assess. The presented results appear to be a reformulation of existing results from
stochastic thermodynamics rather than a fundamentally new force-flux relationship.
On practical utility and examples
The examples, including the “truck” model (Eq. 4), remain somewhat unconvincing as demonstrations of the framework’s
practical advantages. Once the rates (f’s) and errors (epsilons) are specified, the full dynamics are known, and all relevant
quantities can already be computed. The additional construction of a nonequilibrium “force” that lacks clear physical
interpretation does not appear to provide further insight or predictive power.
On the claimed variational aspect
The critique of Schnakenberg’s approach is reasonable. Nonetheless, it remains unclear why the proposed formalism
constitutes a variational principle. Since the state variables (states, traffics, and fluxes) uniquely specify the system, there
is no remaining inference step or optimization to be performed.
Summary
Overall, while the manuscript presents a technically correct analysis, its conceptual novelty and generality remain uncertain.
The work may be of interest to specialists in stochastic thermodynamics or statistical physics, but its broader relevance is
limited. I therefore recommend that the manuscript be considered for publication in a more technically oriented journal such
as Physical Review E or Journal of Statistical Physics, where the detailed formalism can be more thoroughly examined.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have successfully addressed the main issues raised in the first review. The revised manuscript now clearly
defines its scope, strengthens its theoretical consistency, and improves readability. The presentation of the Caliber Force
Theory is much clearer, and the relation to existing frameworks such as Maximum Caliber and Stochastic Thermodynamics
is well clarified. The mathematical structure is now rigorous, the notation is consistent, and the examples are properly
explained. The manuscript is internally consistent and scientifically sound. We recommend publication.

### Reviewer 3

The Authors' replies and modifications, both to my comments and to those of the other reviewers, are appropriate and
sensible. The rewritten paper is better explained and easier to read. Several of the explanatory insertions made in reply to
other reviewer comments are quite helpful to a more thorough and systematic framing of the arguments. I am happy to
recommend that the paper be published in its current form.
There are still some typos -- duplicated text and other marks of revision fatigue -- but hopefully the typesetters will catch most
of those. Here are two:
l.561 applies -> applied
l.872-873, repeated "in the present work"

### Reviewer 4

For the original manuscript, we were concerned that the derivation of the theoretical framework lacked theoretical rigor due to an inappropriate analogy to equilibrium thermodynamics. In the revised manuscript, the authors have removed this
confusing analogy and presented a much more rigorous formulation of their force and caliber under non-equilibrium
conditions. In particular, it is well known that the caliber in equilibrium systems equals path entropy. However, their definition
of “caliber” in the non-equilibrium system is fundamentally different, i.e., they include an additional
restrictive term related to the coordinates (Eq. 4), and these coordinates were derived from their First Law. It would be helpful if the authors could include more explicit
discussions on this point. In addition, we would suggest the authors to include their explanation of the difference between M_12 and M_13 (Fig. M1a) in their revised manuscript. Overall, we would like to recommend the
publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications. Further review is not needed.

## Paper

## Abstract

The great power of equilibrium statistical physics comes from its principled foundations: its First Law (conservation), Second Law (variational tendency principle), and its Legendre Transforms from observables (U,V,N) to their driving forces (T,p,µ). Here, we generalize this structure to nonequilibria in Caliber Force Theory, replacing state entropies with path entropies; and replacing (U,V,N) with dynamic observables (node probabilities, edge traffics, and cycle fluxes). Caliber Force Theory derives dynamical forces and a complete set of conjugate relations: (i) It yields generalized Maxwell-Onsager relations and fluctuation-response relations, applicable far from equilibrium; (ii) It constructs dynamical models from mixed force-observable constraints; and (iii) It reveals relationships—including a generalized Einstein relation, an “equal-traffic” rule for optimizing molecular motors, and a “third Kirchhoff’s law” of stochastic transport—and can resolve some dynamical paradoxes.

---

## Introduction

Nonequilibrium (NEQ) statistical physics has not yet had the same level of solid and general grounding in foundational principles as equilibrium (EQ) statistical physics has had.1

In EQ physics,2,3 a phase space is represented by a complete set of observables such as (U,V,N) and is subject to conservation (First Law) and an entropic tendency (Second Law). Legendre Transforms then derive the conjugated force variables, such as (1/T,p/T, −µ/T), as well as Maxwell Relations and near-EQ fluctuation-response relations. These conjugates are forces insofar as they are derivatives of the underlying variational potential, the entropy. Examples of the practical manifestations of EQ physics are: (1) Computing forces is essential in modeling molecules; their net balance identifies stable states and dominant populations. (2) Maxwell Relations give conversions to compute experimentally realizable properties from theoretical model quantities such as S(U). In addition, early theories of NEQ took their cue from EQ, starting from (U,V,N) or (T,p,µ) and the First and Second Laws of EQ, but in so doing such models were limited to near or local-EQ processes, e.g., requiring baths to be fast-equilibrating for well-defined T and µ.4,5

We develop a framework of principles for NEQ statistical physics, which we call Caliber Force Theory (CFT). In important ways, it resembles the framework of EQ: it entails a conservation law; a variational tendency principle; Legendre Transforms that give forces; Maxwell-like relations among forces and observables; and fluctuation-response relations. However, for NEQ, we require two main differences relative to EQ theory. First, the Second-Law-like variational principle for NEQ is Maximum Caliber (Max Cal),6–9 maximizing an entropy over pathways, not Maximum Entropy, maximizing an entropy over states. Second, the complete set of observables is not the (U,V,N) quantities of EQ theory, but rather (π,τ,J), where πs are state probabilities at the nodes; τs are the total flux activity (“traffic”10,11) along the edges, and Js are net fluxes around the cycles.12,13 An essential result of the present paper is the construction of a non-degenerate basis for these observables, forming a proper coordinate system that is required for their Legendre transforms.

We note that both NEQ and EQ physics have two main levels of usage: call them micro and macro. In micro, in EQ statistical mechanics, you build a probabilistic model: Given a microscopic state space, maximize the state entropy (as a functional of distributions) and infer the Boltzmann state distribution. In macro, in EQ thermodynamics, you are given a macroscopic function S(U,V,N), and you use mathematical transforms to compute relations between forces, observables and constraints, irrespective of the underlying model. The two situations both utilize Maximum Entropy (Max Ent), but in different ways: In micro, Max Ent gives distribution functions; in macro, it defines forces. NEQ physics has parallels to these two usages: Max Cal is used for model-making, while CFT, developed here, gives forces and mathematics for force-observable-constraint relations.

## Results

Establishing the Two Laws

First, we require a complete set of variables that can characterize NEQ steady states (NESS) (see Method A for why steady state). In EQ thermodynamics, the First Law is a principle of complete parameterization for conserved quantities. In particular, energy is a conserved quantity of an underlying Hamiltonian dynamics. And energy conservation can occur through internal (U), mechanical (V), or chemical (N) forms; these define a complete set. In EQ physics, these macroscopic variables (U,V,N) are sufficient to specify the full EQ microstate probability distribution because microstates within an energy shell have equal probability (Liouville’s theorem).

Here instead, for NESS stochastic flows (e.g. for Markov jump processes on a network in Fig. 1a), what is conserved is the flowing agent itself, represented by the conservation of its state probabilities, π . These probabilities π describe the time fractions of the agent occupying each state (node) in the long term, but they do not describe the agent’s transition statistics. A complete set of observables for NESS is: x = (π ,τ ,J ) (Fig. 1b). The second type of observables needed is the total flux on each edge: we follow Maes et al. to call the sum of forward plus backward flows the traffic.10,11 The traffic τ and the probability distribution π are exclusive as an agent can have the same π but different τ simply by having different transition timescales. The last type of observables needed is the net flows on the network, which must be cyclic because net inflow to a node must balance the outflow at NESS. The cycle flux J , too, is distinct because J describes the net flow whereas τ is the total flow and π is not about flow. See Method B on why we take these observables to be fundamental.

There are some considerations in choosing the variables. First, note that generic Markov stochastic flows do not have the same Liouville symmetry as Hamiltonian systems at EQ. Therefore, we need the complete set of mesoscopic observables (π ,τ ,J ) in order to fully parameterize a generic Markov dynamics. Time scale separation is to Markov dynamics what Liouville symmetry is to Hamiltonian dynamics—it is important that these coordinates be non-degenerate. The vector of node probabilities, π , omits one probability (from a chosen reference node, m) to handle normalization, while the net fluxes are described by a linearly-independent basis of fundamental cycle fluxes (see Method B), J , to handle steady-state flux conservation.12,13 These considerations give a relationship for the transition rates k (from node i to j) of the Markov jump process:

k = (τ +J ) / (2π ) (1)

where edge net fluxes J is spanned by the (fundamental) cycle fluxes J and the edge traffic τ = τ is the time-symmetric, total flux activity of the edge ij. See Method B for the steps to construct x = (π ,τ ,J ). The dimension parsing here is similar to the landscape-flux decomposition in Markov diffusion processes.14–17

Next, we seek a tendency principle for NEQ. For Equilibria, the tendencies are described by the adiabatic inaccessibility from Carathéodory, or Clausius’ inequality, or Boltzmann’s H theorem for irreversible relaxation, and/or the variational principle of Maximum Entropy (Max Ent) over microscopic states that “derives” the Boltzmann EQ distribution (Gibbs and Jaynes). Here, we seek notions of forces that govern NEQ tendencies. For EQ, such notions are derived from Max Ent; For NEQ, we thus assert instead the principle of Maximum Caliber (Max Cal),6–9 which says that maximizing the path entropy is to dynamics what maximizing the state entropy is to the static, EQ distribution.5 For a NESS Markov process with transition rate k , the path entropy takes the following form as a functional of path probabilities P (ω ) for length-t trajectories ω , reference to a “doldrum” process with unit transition rates u = 1:

s (x) = lim (1/t) \sum P (ω ) ln [P (ω ) / P (ω )] (2a)
= \sum [p (x) - π (x) - p (x) ln p (x) / π (x)] (2b)

the (one-way) probability edge flux p (x) = [τ + J (J )] / 2 is a function of the traffic (the symmetric part of p , τ = p + p ) and the cycle fluxes (J ). See Method C for a more technical justification of the Two-Law generalizations described above.

Deriving Nonequilibrium Forces

Next, for NEQ, we establish the forces that are conjugate to the observables. For EQ, forces are given by derivatives of the variational tendency quantity; namely the state entropy in that case. Here, for NEQ, the relevant variational quantity is the path entropy, s (x). We define the conjugate forces, F, as their derivatives. Hence, Caliber Force Theory (CFT) gives the following forces for node dwelling, edge exchange, and directed cycle completion (Method D) as:

F = - ∂s / ∂π = \sum (k - 1) - \sum (k - 1) (3)
F = - ∂s / ∂τ = 1/2 ln (k / k ) (3)
F = - ∂s / ∂J = 1/2 ln (k k ... k / k k ... k ) (3)

where i i ... i i is the state sequence of the cycle c and, as usual, partial derivatives ∂s (x)/∂x compute slopes holding other x' in x fixed. Equations (3) are a main result of the present paper: a rigorous way to derive NEQ forces for network steady states from a variational principle, and their dependence on network rates.

At this point, it is worth touching base with the related research area of Stochastic Thermodynamics (ST), which has sought a variational definition of forces since Prigogine.18–20 Lacking such a principle, ST adopted the cycle affinity.12,13,21 While that correctly identifies the breaking of detailed balance (Kolmogorov’s criterion) and matches energetic driving in EQ-bath-driven systems (Local Detailed Balance), it remains ad hoc in the sense that it is not derived as the derivative of a variational potential. CFT supplies this missing variational basis. First, CFT shows that ST’s cycle affinity is exactly twice the value of the path entropy derivative (its cycle force). Second, CFT shows that its variational cycle force reduces to half the energetic form of cycle affinity, (∆µ - w)/(k T), only in the limit of fast-equilibrating baths.

Compare again to EQ physics for a moment. For EQ, the maximization of entropy (for fixed U) can be alternatively expressed as minimization of the free energy (for fixed T). Similarly for NEQ, a change of constraints leads from maximization of path entropy to maximization of the Caliber c(F), obtained from the Legendre transform of path entropy. This now gives a duality between the force and observable coordinates:

c(F) = F · x + s (x) (4)

Hence, maximizing the Caliber is equivalent to maximizing path entropy that is constrained by observables x, and where the forces F are the Lagrange multipliers. Physically, Eq. (4) separates the potential into the “energetic part” F · x for tendency and activity bias and the “entropic part” s (x) capturing the likelihood of observing x in the uniform and unit-active doldrum process before any symmetry-breaking forces are applied.22 Here, instead of following Jaynes’ convention,6 we follow Pressé et al. to call the Legendre transform of the path entropy the Caliber, as a free-energy-like function.8 Also, in direct analogy to the free energy for equilibria, the Caliber is the (scaled) logarithm of the dynamical partition function:

c(F) = lim (1/t) ln \sum P (ω ) e^(F · X(ω )) (5)

where X(ω ) is the vector of time-extensive counting path observables whose long-term average rates are the observable coordinate x (see Method B for explicit expressions). Large Deviation Theory (LDT) has provided a simple way to compute the Caliber (Method E):1,23–25 it is the largest eigenvalue of “the tilted matrix”, constructed by “tilting” the transition rate matrix of the doldrum process with the forces.

Nonequilibrium Fluctuation-Response Relations

The conjugate observable-force relations of equilibrium thermodynamics give rise to the Maxwell symmetry relationships. Again we have here for NEQ corresponding symmetry relations. The dual-potential structure empowers our framework. The path entropy transforms observables to forces (Eq. 3), while the Caliber gives the reverse:

x(F) = ∂c / ∂F (6)

This structure immediately yields a complete set of universal response laws. The second derivatives of the Caliber produce the Fluctuation-Susceptibility Equalities, which include the far-from-EQ generalizations of Maxwell relations at EQ and Onsager reciprocality near EQ:26

∂x / ∂F = ∂^2c / ∂F^2 = lim (Var[X] / t) > 0 (7a)
∂x / ∂F' = ∂x' / ∂F = ∂^2c / ∂F ∂F' = lim (CoV[X,X'] / t) (7b)

where Var and CoV represent variance and covariance, X, X' can be any two of the counting variables X, x, x' are their average rates, and F, F' are their conjugated forces.

Response relations (7a) and (7b) are useful because (a) the forces have the property of locality, i.e., they relate only to the given node, or edge, or cycle (see Eqs. 3); and (b) the full set of forces constitutes a complete coordinate. Therefore, when a set of transition rates are changed, dk, upon varying physical properties, e.g. concentrations of reactants or energy barriers, this tunes a few localized forces, allowing for the responses in x to be computed in terms of the local force variations,

dx = \sum (∂x / ∂F) · (∂F / ∂k) dk (8)

The NEQ Maxwell-Onsager and fluctuation-susceptibility equalities then govern the responses, providing generic sign and symmetry predictions on the susceptibilities ∂x/∂F and generalizing known near-EQ, linear-response results.

A power of equilibrium physics is the ability to work with useful combinations of observables and forces by swapping conjugate variables, such as getting (T,V,N) from (U,V,N). We have the same power here. For a mixed coordinate z = (F , x ) obtained by switching out conjugate variables, e.g. swapping J with F so that F = F and x = (π , τ ), partial Legendre transforms define the corresponding potential ϕ(z):

ϕ = F · x + s (9a)
-ϕ = F · x - c (9b)

The remaining unknown variables are its derivatives under the mixed coordinate z:

x (z) = ∂ϕ / ∂F ; F (z) = - ∂ϕ / ∂x (10)

The underlying transition rates k can then be computed by combining Eq. (10) with Eq. (1). This ability to compute new transition rates when constraints of forces or observables are changed directly generalizes traditional Max Cal inference,6–9 which was limited to observable constraints.

The universal response laws extend to mixed coordinates too. Maxwell-Onsager Relations directly follow from Eq. (10). And, the Fluctuation-Susceptibility Equalities can also be derived. The response of the conjugate variables (x , F ) to perturbations in the mixed coordinates z are given by the covariances (Method G):

[∂x / ∂F ∂x / ∂x] = [C C ] [I 0]
[∂F / ∂F ∂F / ∂x] [C C ] [0 -C^-1]

Here, C is a N -by-N covariance matrix of the components of X ; C is that of X ; C is a N -by-N matrix with covariance terms between X and X ; And, C = C equals the transpose of C .

Below are four examples to illustrate applications of CFT: a machine driven to Far From Equilibrium; optimizing a machine under constraints; uncovering a stochastic transport law; and resolving a traffic paradox.

A. How Far is Far From Equilibrium?

First, here is a toy model sufficiently simple to illustrate: (a) how to characterize distance from equilibrium with the cycles force in CFT; (b) the transition of force-flow relations from linear to nonlinear; and (c) the convergence to EQ in the limit of a slow motor. Fig. 2a shows a three-state Markov model. The three forward rates all equal f; the three back rates all equal b; the process is a 1-dimensional biased random walk; and we are given f > b, an intrinsic drive to spin in the direction of the bold arrows that is not part of the modeled aspects here. So, f/b is an order parameter: f/b ≫ 1 is fast spinning while f/b → 1 is the limit of slow near-EQ spinning.

The angular velocity is the cumulative angular displacement divided by total travel time, ω = ∆Θ/t, and its average angular velocity ⟨ω⟩ is 2πJ where J = (f - b)/3. Further, for 1-D diffusion, the diffusion coefficient D is defined by the long-term variance of the cumulative angular displacement, Var[∆Θ] ∼ 2Dt, leading to D = lim (Var[∆Θ] / 2t) = lim (t Var[ω] / 2). Thus, taking Eq. (7a) for cycle flux J = ⟨ω⟩/(2π) gives

∂⟨ω⟩ / ∂F = 2π ∂J / ∂F = 2π lim (t Var[ω]) = D / π (12)

According to Eqs. (3), the forces are F = (3/2) log(f/b), F = (1/2) log(f/b), and F = 0 due to rotational symmetry. Hence, the partial derivatives on the left of Eq. (12) corresponds to tuning the bias f/b while keeping the activity f b fixed—physically realized, for instance, by changing the ADP/ATP concentration ratios or the rotational torque from the F part of the ATPase.

Now, the average rotational speed ⟨ω⟩ = 2π(f - b)/3 can be expressed in terms of the force coordinate, and for small F , ⟨ω⟩ ≈ µF with the mobility µ satisfying the Einstein relations µ ≈ D/π. Therefore, Eq. (12) from CFT is the nonlinear, far-from-EQ generalization of Einstein relation, and it tells us that ⟨ω⟩ increases with F nonlinearly because the diffusivity D increases with the cycle forces too (Fig. 2b). See Method F for analytical verification.

B. Optimizing Molecular Devices: A Noise Relationship

In this example, we show how CFT brings capabilities to design and optimize network flows that have not been available before. Consider a simple cycle, say the 2-step molecular motor in Fig 3a, that takes in ATP in one step and performs an action in the other step. Traditionally, you would make a Markov State Model with rates k , and you could vary those rates to maximize speed or power27,28 or minimize fluctuations.29,30. But, now consider the challenge of design and optimization in the presence of constraints, or to study relationships more analytically among rate variables, even nonlinear ones. For example, how can you maximize the motor’s speed (i.e., its cycle flux, J) given a fixed energy source (e.g., a constant ATP/ADP ratio, a fixed cycle force, F ) and given fixed traffic (forward plus back fluxes)?

Prior work can compute average speed or fluctuations from the transition rates k , using Hill’s diagram method12,13 or generating functions.29,31 What’s added here is defined forces, their relationships to their observables, and the math to give relationships among them under constraints.

In particular, Fig. 3b shows a result from CFT, namely the Equal Traffic Principle, for the unicircular process above. (Details are derived in Method H): At a fixed cycle force and given total traffic (sum of all edge traffics), the cycle flux J (the motor’s speed) is maximized when the traffic is distributed equally among all edges in the cycle, illustrated in (Fig. 3b). This holds regardless of the state populations (π), revealing a degenerate optimum. Furthermore, CFT allows for optimization under multiple constraints, showing how fluctuations in this model can be minimized by equal traffic even when the motor is constrained to operate with highly asymmetric state populations (π ≈ 1) (Fig. 3c), a feature needed for motors like myosin.32,33

C. A “Third Kirchhoff’s Law” for Stochastic Transport

In this example, we show how CFT brings insights about fluctuations on networks where the macroscopic flow behaviors are known. Kirchhoff’s two laws for electrical circuits describe the conservation of current at nodes and that the voltage sums to zero around loops. But these are macroscopic laws that consider only average forward flow rates and don’t address the underlying stochastic back-stepping of the mobile carrier agents that can occur at small flow rates or for small agent numbers. For transport that is stochastic, where fluctuations can be significant, CFT derives a third relationship.

Prior work that has introduced stochastic fluctuations into network flows34–36 is limited in two ways. First, it utilizes a relationship between net fluxes (J), state probabilities (π), and driving potentials analogous to a battery’s voltage. The potentials, can be related to CFT’s cycle force (F ) but only under the assumption of Local Detailed Balance. Second, that description, which is based solely on (π,J,F ), is fundamentally incomplete. In contrast, CFT gives a proper and complete set of coordinates, including edge traffic (τ) and edge force (F ).

To illustrate the value, we show here how the CFT framework derives a “third Kirchhoff’s Law” for stochastic transport, a rule that governs network flows where fluctuations are significant. Consider a system where particles can traverse between two points A and B via multiple parallel channels (Fig. 4a). In this example, we denote the forward rates from B to A through channel i as f and the reverse as r (not k for brevity). When the two “battery-channel cycles” are driven out of equilibrium by equal cycle forces, CFT provides a simple and elegant rule. Here, the equal-cycle-force condition corresponds to an equal level of asymmetry in the channels with the forward rates and reverse satisfying f /r = f /r . From this, we show that the ratio of net fluxes (J /J ) through the two channels is identical to the ratio of their traffics (τ /τ ), and both are determined by the exponential of their respective edge forces (Method I):

J / J = τ / τ = e^F / e^F = sqrt(f / r ) / sqrt(f / r ) (13)

This result establishes the edge force as the fundamental quantity governing both the allocation of directed flow and the underlying stochastic activity in symmetrically driven networks, adding a principle to transport laws where fluctuations are important.

D. CFT Forces Can Resolve Dynamical Paradoxes

In much of physics, it is better to work with forces than with displacements or velocities. This is because when different actions matter, their forces sum together to tell more complete stories. Force-based modeling can resolve cooperation and conflict among different actions. A key value of CFT is its principled definitions and completeness of sets of forces of different types of network flows. Neglecting any of the three components—e.g. focus narrowly on π, J, and F —can lead to apparent “paradoxes.”

In prior work, the cycle flux J is often paired with the cycle affinity (2 F ) because their product gives the entropy production rate.12,13 One might expect these two components to be positively correlated. However, it is important to recognize that they are distinct, as CFT does, because such correlation is not guaranteed unless other degrees of freedom are fixed appropriately. In this section, we give an example of truck delivers on a simple network to illustrate how CFT resolves this puzzle of forces and flows by proper accounting of other degrees of freedom.

Consider two truck drivers, Alice and Bob, both delivering a product; see (Fig. 5a). The two drivers have delivery rates f and f′, but they also have error rates (backrates) ϵf and ϵf′. If Bob—who has the higher error rate than Alice (ϵ′ > ϵ)—increases his delivery rate (f′), then the overall net flux of deliveries (J ) from the team of two drivers increases, as expected. However, in contrast, the conjugate cycle force (F ), which is often regarded as the sole driver of the flux, simultaneously decreases (Fig. 5b). This anti-correlation between a flux and its putative driving force cannot be explained if you only account for the force and flux of the cycle alone. The paradox is resolved within CFT by recognizing the crucial role of the edge force, F . As Bob works faster (tuning the physical rate parameter f′), he is effectively tuning two forces simultaneously: the total edge force increases, while the cycle force decreases. A full decomposition of the response in the force coordinate shows that the positive contribution from the increasing edge force overwhelms the negative contribution from the decreasing cycle force (Method J):

dJ / df' = 2 (∂J / ∂F ) (∂F / ∂f') + 2 (∂J / ∂F ) (∂F / ∂f') (14)

This example shows the importance of completeness in a dynamical description, since a perturbation of a network can change multiple network forces.
